% I'm not sure if I would define a formula. Just displaying the deltas together could be enough

% \cite{efficiencyRatio} suggests something similar. It is defined as Acc/energy, which seems like a pretty limited definition.


\subsection{Threats to Validity}
% We only scope in SNNs, it might not generalize to other domains

% Our input from practicioners come from a concrete SNN project. Their views are shaped by this project and mignt not apply to other projects

The nature of this study presents some limitations.
Firstly, we focus our scope on SNNs, and specifically on implantable healthcare devices.
Therefore, our findings might not generalize to other domains of AI.
In general, we believe most of our reflections could be applied to the field of edge AI, given the similarities between both fields.
Edge AI also deals with low-power devices and sometimes with devices running on a battery.
Additionally, some reflections could be applied to the field of Green AI in general, since these metrics focus on reporting energy consumption.
However, the definition and validity of these metrics for other fields or applications would have to be evaluated independently.

The lens of the project through which we study the problem also limits the feedback from the practitioners.
These practitioners come from a concrete neuromorphic project from the SELF Lab.
Their views are shaped by this project, and some conclusions might not apply to other projects.

% Collection methodology. Little literature/research on this topic (benchmarking SNNs). Research is very recent, there could be more work in the future that tackles this problems. The first look into it is from 2023
The limited research done in SNN benchmarking is also a limiting factor for the collection methodology applied for this review.
The research and first attempts at benchmark standardization started as recently as 2023.
Therefore, there is little literature to apply a systematic method, so we performed an ad hoc literature review. To mitigate problems derived from this method, we applied snowballing over the Neurobench paper \cite{yik2025neurobenchframeworkbenchmarkingneuromorphic} to cover a larger number of relevant papers.
Additionally, there could be new research that tackles these problems in the near future.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
Neuromorphic computing and SNNs are a promising new paradigm for improving the energy efficiency of Artificial Intelligence models.
However, as highlighted in this study, the research has focused mainly on evaluating hardware and models in conjunction, while research into only model benchmarking is relatively new.

By looking into the works that focus on SNN benchmarking, we uncovered and categorized the most common metrics for assessing the energy consumption of an SNN model, based on Accessibility, Fidelity, and Actionability
With this classification, we identified which metrics approximate energy consumption better and are easier to measure during model development.

We find out that there are no energy metrics that are both Accessible and present High Fidelity.
Benchmarking frameworks for SNNs focus mainly on model design and metrics, without considering the effects of target hardware.
This makes early evaluation of the model difficult, and we recommend research directions towards building reliable estimations that bridge Accessibility and Fidelity.

The study also highlighted the lack of actionable metrics for developers. Despite the variety of metrics, none of them focused on giving the developer early and approachable feedback.
Therefore, from the lenses of implantable neuromorphic devices, we proposed research directions to extend the catalog with actionable metrics, focusing on accurately and transparently representing energy and power trends during development, estimated battery life, and Energy-Accuracy tradeoff.

By identifying gaps in existing energy metrics for SNNs in neuromorphic implants and proposing research directions to bridge them, this study lays the groundwork for more effective benchmarking methods. 
Our recommendations open future research into energy metrics that provide quicker feedback and better Actionability, ultimately supporting developers in designing more efficient and practical SNN models.

title: On using AI for EEG-based BCI applications: problems, current challenges and future trends
summary:
Imagine unlocking the power of the mind to communicate, create, and even
interact with the world around us. Recent breakthroughs in Artificial
Intelligence (AI), especially in how machines "see" and "understand" language,
are now fueling exciting progress in decoding brain signals from scalp
electroencephalography (EEG). Prima facie, this opens the door to revolutionary
brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) designed for real life, moving beyond
traditional uses to envision Brain-to-Speech, Brain-to-Image, and even a
Brain-to-Internet of Things (BCIoT).
  However, the journey is not as straightforward as it was for Computer Vision
(CV) and Natural Language Processing (NLP). Applying AI to real-world EEG-based
BCIs, particularly in building powerful foundational models, presents unique
and intricate hurdles that could affect their reliability.
  Here, we unfold a guided exploration of this dynamic and rapidly evolving
research area. Rather than barely outlining a map of current endeavors and
results, the goal is to provide a principled navigation of this hot and
cutting-edge research landscape. We consider the basic paradigms that emerge
from a causal perspective and the attendant challenges presented to AI-based
models. Looking ahead, we then discuss promising research avenues that could
overcome today's technological, methodological, and ethical limitations. Our
aim is to lay out a clear roadmap for creating truly practical and effective
EEG-based BCI solutions that can thrive in everyday environments.

title: REMS: a unified solution representation, problem modeling and metaheuristic algorithm design for general combinatorial optimization problems
summary:
Combinatorial optimization problems (COPs) with discrete variables and finite
search space are critical across numerous fields, and solving them in
metaheuristic algorithms is popular. However, addressing a specific COP
typically requires developing a tailored and handcrafted algorithm. Even minor
adjustments, such as constraint changes, may necessitate algorithm
redevelopment. Therefore, establishing a framework for formulating diverse COPs
into a unified paradigm and designing reusable metaheuristic algorithms is
valuable. A COP can be typically viewed as the process of giving resources to
perform specific tasks, subjecting to given constraints. Motivated by this, a
resource-centered modeling and solving framework (REMS) is introduced for the
first time. We first extract and define resources and tasks from a COP.
Subsequently, given predetermined resources, the solution structure is unified
as assigning tasks to resources, from which variables, objectives, and
constraints can be derived and a problem model is constructed. To solve the
modeled COPs, several fundamental operators are designed based on the unified
solution structure, including the initial solution, neighborhood structure,
destruction and repair, crossover, and ranking. These operators enable the
development of various metaheuristic algorithms. Specially, 4
single-point-based algorithms and 1 population-based algorithm are configured
herein. Experiments on 10 COPs, covering routing, location, loading,
assignment, scheduling, and graph coloring problems, show that REMS can model
these COPs within the unified paradigm and effectively solve them with the
designed metaheuristic algorithms. Furthermore, REMS is more competitive than
GUROBI and SCIP in tackling large-scale instances and complex COPs, and
outperforms OR-TOOLS on several challenging COPs.

	\IEEEPARstart{C}{ombinatorial} optimization problems (COPs) with discrete decision variables and finite search spaces are widely encountered and hold significant importance across various fields \cite{du1998handbook}, including logistics, engineering, economy, healthcare, etc.. A COP can be formulated as \cite{karimi2022machine}
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:COP}
	\begin{array}{l}
	{\rm{min     }} {\kern 5pt} f(\vec x)\\
	{\rm{s.t.   }}{\kern 5pt}G(\vec x) \le 0,H(\vec x) = 0
	\end{array},
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	where $\vec x = \{ {x_1}, \cdots ,{x_n}\}$ denotes variables, ${x_i} \in \Omega_i \subset {\mathbb{Z}^n},{\kern 4pt}i \in \{ 1, \cdots ,n\} $ and $\Omega_i$ is a discrete and finite variable space for $x_i$. $G(\vec x) \le 0$ and $H(\vec x) = 0$ are the inequality and equality constraints, respectively. Put all possible feasible solutions into $\mathcal{F}$, then solving such a COP is to find a solution $\vec x^{*} \in \mathcal{F}$ to enable $f(\vec x^{*}) \le f(\vec x),{\kern 5pt}\forall \vec x \in \mathcal{F}$.
	
	In the real world, addressing evolving needs and requirements necessitates adapting variables $\vec x$, objective functions $f(\vec x)$, as well as constraints $G(\vec x)$ and $H(\vec x)$. It gives rise to various classical COPs such as routing \cite{fleckenstein2023recent, li2022overview}, location \cite{wang2021emergency, lei2023chaotic}, loading \cite{ekici2023large}, assignment \cite{krumke2013generalized}, scheduling \cite{dauzere2024flexible, gao2019review}, and graph coloring problems \cite{jensen2011graph}, along with their variants \cite{kaya2022review}. They generally belong to NP-hard problems \cite{kaya2022review}.
	
	Researchers have dedicated considerable effort to constructing an appropriate model for a COP under a specific context and designing effective solving algorithms including exact and heuristic methods \cite{marti2022exact, griffis2012metaheuristics} based on problem-specific characteristics. In addition, expressing a broad range of COPs into a unified formal paradigm and developing algorithms to address them are also critical pursuits \cite{pagnozzi2019automatic, kallestad2023general, marti202450}, which facilitates the emergence of various generic solvers and related research.
	
	Exact algorithm-based solvers, such as GUROBI, CPLEX, SCIP \cite{eifler2023computational}, CLPK, COIN-OR, and CBC, already possess the capability to express various COPs into unified paradigms and solve them without requiring the redesign of algorithms. They generally model every COP into a strictly defined model structure of mixed integer programming. Hereafter, an exact algorithm like a branch and bound method \cite{lawler1966branch} is employed to solve the constructed model. The solvers typically possess good performance in simple and small-scale COPs. Nevertheless, certain challenges persist. First, some problems may lack a well-structured mathematical formulation such as vehicle routing problems \cite{marti202450}. Modeling for such a COP requires advanced expertise. Second, exact algorithm-based solvers are incapable of modeling and addressing COPs involving nonlinear operators, like ${a^x}$, $\ln x$, higher-order or trigonometric functions, in their objective functions or constraints. Furthermore, the performance of exact algorithms themselves deteriorates as problem complexity and scale increase. 
	
	Heuristic algorithms are typically designed for specific problems, aiming to find reasonable solutions within an acceptable computational burden. 
	They can be broadly categorized into classical heuristic algorithms and metaheuristic algorithms. Classical heuristic algorithms include Greedy Algorithms \cite{zhao2021iterated}, Clarke-Wright Algorithm  \cite{nelson1985implementation}, and Sweep Algorithms \cite{laporte2000classical}, while metaheuristic algorithms encompass Simulated Annealing (SA) \cite{tian1999application}, Tabu Search (TS) \cite{chelouah2000tabu}, Large Neighborhood Search (LNS) \cite{mara2022survey}, Variable Neighborhood Search(VNS) \cite{brimberg2023variable}, and Genetic Algorithm (GA) \cite{zhao2024pega}. Metaheuristic algorithms generally possess better global search capabilities compared to classical heuristic methods \cite{peres2021combinatorial}.
	
	When addressing a COP by heuristic algorithms, an overwhelming majority of related research concentrates on developing dedicated algorithms tailored to specific COPs. Even if a minor variation to a COP, such as changes in constraints, can make the original algorithm inefficient or even inappropriate, leading to the requirement of redesigning the algorithm. The process is typically tedious and time-consuming. If general COPs can be expressed within a unified paradigm like exact algorithm-based solvers, it can effectively avoid redesigning the algorithms and enhance their generality and reusability.
	
	Several heuristic algorithm-based solvers have expressed COPs into a unified paradigm and developed general heuristic methods for solving COPs, with Google's CP-SAT in OR-TOOLS \cite{moreira2024cp}, Hexaly, and OptaPlanner being notable examples. They model COPs into constraint satisfaction problems \cite{brailsford1999constraint} by a specific modeling language and employ various algorithms to solve these models. Among them, CP-SAT adopts conflict-driven clause learning \cite{marques2021conflict} to optimize problems, where it integrates several heuristic search strategies, like Feasibility Pump and LNS, to explore the solution space. Hexaly introduces list variables to improve modeling and solving for routing and scheduling problems. It provides heuristic algorithms like local search, population-based methods, and surrogate modeling techniques to optimize problems. OptaPlanner models planning problems by defining problem facts, planning entities, variables, and both soft and hard constraints. It employs a penalty function method to assess solutions and designs metaheuristic methods, such as TS, LNS, and VNS, for solving problems. Notably, certain solvers, like CP-SAT and Hexaly, incorporate the exact algorithms to improve performance. Similarly, some exact algorithm-based solvers, like GUROBI and CPLEX, also integrate heuristic rules to enhance performance.
	
	Additionally, there are some heuristic algorithm-based solvers being tailored for specific types of COPs. For instance, the Routing Solver and Knapsack Solver in OR-Tools specialize in vehicle routing and knapsack problems, respectively, each providing tailored modeling and heuristic methods based on their specific problem knowledge. Furthermore, certain researchers have devoted themselves to designing general and effective heuristic algorithms for one particular type of COPs \cite{pagnozzi2019automatic, vidal2014unified, blum2016construct, sarafraz2021unified, shi2024fixed}. 
	
	However, despite these efforts, the research on problem representation and general heuristic algorithms remains limited, particularly regarding metaheuristic algorithms, as seen in \cite{marti202450}. Moreover, the relative research still encounters challenges. For example, due to the limitations of modeling and solving methods, some heuristic algorithm-based solvers struggle to effectively model and solve for the highly nonlinear objectives and constraints, such as high-order polynomials, non-convex, logarithmic, exponential, and power functions. 
	
	%research on heuristic algorithm-based solvers remains limited, particularly regarding metaheuristic algorithms \cite{marti202450}. 
	%heuristic algorithm-based solvers and the relative research still encounter challenges. Concerning the modeling, some heuristic algorithm-based solvers fail to model for the highly nonlinear objectives and constraints, such as high-order polynomials, non-convex, logarithmic, exponential, and power functions. Overall, research on heuristic algorithm-based solvers remains limited, particularly regarding metaheuristic algorithms \cite{marti202450}. 
	
	We find that COPs typically can be viewed as the process that gives resources to performing certain tasks. With this point of view, COPs can be uniformly described as how to appropriately arrange the tasks for the resources subjecting to necessary constraints. Inspired by this, we propose a resource-centered modeling and solving framework (REMS). This framework expresses general COPs within a unified paradigm, facilitating the development of diverse operators, which further enables the configuration of metaheuristic algorithms to address COPs modeled within this paradigm. REMS enriches the research about problem representation and provides guidance for the design of general metaheuristic methods.
	
	The main contribution of the paper is as follows.
	
	\begin{itemize}
		\item A resource-centered problem representation paradigm for general COPs is introduced for the first time. The paradigm unifies the solution structure by assigning tasks to resources within a predetermined resource set. Based on the unified structure, variables, objective functions, and constraints can be defined, enabling the representation of diverse COPs in a unified form. Furthermore, several frequently used objective functions and constraints are identified by further extracting the general knowledge of COPs.
		
		\item Several operators and metaheuristic algorithms are developed to solve COPs modeled in REMS. Based on the unified solution structure, several fundamental operators are designed for constructing various metaheuristic algorithms. An initial solution is constructed by incrementally inserting feasible tasks into resources. The optimization operators, including neighbor structure, destroy, repair, and crossover, are designed to search the solution space. Meanwhile, a ranking method for feasible and infeasible solutions is employed. In particular, these operators are integrated into single-point-based and population-based algorithm frameworks, resulting in algorithms such as SA, LNS, VNS, TS, and GA.
		%	 \cite{maier2014evolutionary}
		
		\item Experiments conducted on 10 COPs show that REMS can model and solve various COPs, and exhibits competitive performance in handling large-scale instances and complex problems than GUROBI, SCIP, and OR-TOOLS. 10 COPs from routing, location, assignment, packing, scheduling, and graph coloring problems are employed for the experimental study. The extensive experiment results reveal that REMS can effectively model and solve these problems. REMS outperforms GUROBI and SCIP when solving some large-scale instances and complex problems, and surpasses OR-TOOLS in addressing several problems with complex objectives and constraints. Notably, REMS is a generic framework for solving various COPs. With REMS, we only need to pay attention to problem modeling. Once the problem is modeled with the resource-centered paradigm, satisfactory optimization results can be obtained by the configured metaheuristics.
		
		
		
	\end{itemize}

	\section{Resource-centered problem representation method for combinatorial optimization}\label{s2}
	
	\subsection{Motivation}\label{s21}
	
	COPs can be grouped into various categories, with each category featuring different variables, objectives, and constraints. Regardless of the diversity, some common characteristics can be observed and extracted. We find that a COP can be typically viewed as the process of giving resources to perform specific tasks. Accordingly, the core decision, independent of objectives and constraints, can be generally regarded as selecting discrete tasks from one finite task set and assigning them to discrete resources from another finite resource set. For instance, the routing problem needs to assign arcs or points to available vehicles. In the bin packing problem, items are assigned to bins. Job shop scheduling involves assigning jobs to machines, while school timetable scheduling may need to assign courses to teachers. The graph coloring problem aims at assigning colors to nodes. Accordingly, we can extract two key concepts from COPs.
	
	\begin{itemize}
		\item \emph{Task}: Any assignable object can be called a task, such as arcs or points, items, jobs, courses, and colors in the examples mentioned above.
		
		\item \emph{Resource}: A resource is the object to which tasks are assigned. The vehicles, bins, machines, teachers, and nodes can be regarded as resources in terms of the above examples. 
		
	\end{itemize}
	
	Note that there is no clear boundary between resources and tasks for a specific COP, which depends on which type of objects need to be assigned and which type of objects they should be assigned to. For example, concerning a graph coloring problem, if we plan to assign colors to nodes, then the colors are assignable objects and are deemed tasks. And the nodes are objects that the tasks should be assigned to and are regarded as resources. Conversely, if we plan to assign nodes to colors, then nodes can be considered tasks, while colors serve as resources.
	
	%Moreover, resources and tasks may not actually exist in some COPs, but we can assume some virtual resources and tasks to facilitate the modeling and problem-solving process. For instance, we can employ a virtual resource for a classical location problem so that we can assign a series of facility locations (tasks) for it. In a school timetable scheduling, a virtual task can be employed to represent no course is assigned for a teacher in a particular time slot.
	
	Furthermore, when assigning tasks to resources, the tasks should be executed in a specific order in some cases, while in others the execution order does not need to be noticed. Therefore, we assume that each resource has one or more positions to accommodate tasks with one position dedicated to one task, which can either be ordered or unordered. For example, in COPs such as routing, job shop scheduling, and school timetabling scheduling, tasks must be assigned to resources in a specific sequence to ensure chronological execution. In these cases, the resource positions are ordered and carry particular meanings, such as time slots. In contrast, in problems like bin packing and graph coloring, the order of tasks on each resource is unnecessary. The tasks simply need to be assigned to resources, and the positions are unordered.
	
	Referring to the analysis above, solving such a COP is reduced to make the best decision on assigning which task to which resource in which positions to realize a specific objective within given constraints. If the resources are predetermined and fixed, the solution structure can be commonly represented as determining the assigned task to a resource position for the COP. Consequently, by extracting and defining the resources and tasks from a COP, a unified solution structure can be obtained. Based on the unified solution structure, the problem can be further expressed by defining variables, objectives, and constraints to describe the assignment relationship between resources and tasks.
	
	
	\subsection{Modeling Framework and Modeling Elements}\label{s22}
	
	With loss of generality, COPs considered in this paper are assumed to have the following characteristics.
	
	\begin{itemize}
		
		\item  The resources and tasks are discrete and finite.
		
		\item  The resources and tasks are predefined and remain unchanged.
		
	\end{itemize}
	
	The modeling framework is displayed in Fig.~\ref{Fig:modeling framework}, where we first extract and define resources and tasks for a COP, organizing them into sets $R$ and $T$, respectively. Under predetermined resources, the solution structure is consistently represented as assigning tasks to the positions of resources. Within this structure, resources remain fixed, while the tasks from $T$ are arranged to each resource in $R$. We employ $S = \{ {S_1}, \cdots ,{S_m}\} $ to denote the solution structure and $m$ is the number of resources. Among them, $S_i=\{s_{i,1},s_{i,2},\cdots\}$ is the task set assigned to the $i$th resource and $s_{i,k}$ indicates the task located in the $k$th position of the $i$th resource, ${s_{i,k}} \in T$.
	%=====================================================
	\begin{figure}[htb]
		\begin{center}		\subfigure{\psfig{file=figures/framework.eps, width=3.6in}}
		\end{center}
		\caption{Modeling framework of REMS.}\label{Fig:modeling framework}
	\end{figure}
	%======================================================
	
	Based on the unified solution structure, we model various COPs into a unified framework by defining variables, objectives, and constraints. Within them, the variables serve to capture the specific attributes or aspects of the solution structure, including assignment or sequence variable $X$ and attribute variables $Y$. $X$ possesses the same form as the solution structure, explicitly representing the specific tasks assigned to resource positions. When the positions of resources are unordered, the variable serves as an assignment variable, as in the bin packing and graph coloring problems. As the resource positions are ordered, $X$ also reflects the execution sequence of tasks. In this case, it can be regarded as a sequence variable, as seen in timetable scheduling and vehicle routing problems. The attribute variable $Y$ can capture other specific attributes or aspects of the solution structure, such as the start and end times for tasks at resource positions.
	
	The objective $f$ defines the desired outcome of a COP, expressed as the maximization or minimization of a particular performance metric. The constraint $G$ represents limitations or requirements between resources and tasks. Specifically, constraints ensure the matching feasibility between resources and tasks, such as capacity limitation of resources. The objective and constraints can be calculated by the variables $X$ and $Y$.
	
	Hereafter, the key modeling elements will be introduced in detail.
	
	
	\subsubsection{\textcolor{black}{Resource and Task}}\label{s221}
	
	Assume that we can extract $m$ resources and $n$ tasks from a COP, the resource set $R$ can be represented as
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:resource}
	\begin{array}{l}
	R = \{ {R_1},{R_2}, \cdots ,{R_m}\} 
	\end{array},
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	and the task set $T$ can be denoted as
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:task}
	\begin{array}{l}
	T = \{ {T_1},{T_2}, \cdots ,{T_n}\} 
	\end{array},
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	
	Each resource or task is associated with a unique index that distinguishes it from other resources or tasks. Additionally, both resource and task sets may possess one or more attributes, with each resource or task linked with a specific attribute value.
	
	Suppose $R$ has $p$ attributes, then the index and attribute values of ${R_i}$ can be expressed as
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:resouce denote}
	\begin{array}{l}
	(d_i^R,A_{i,1}^R, \cdots ,A_{i,p}^R),{\kern 5pt}i \in \mathcal{I} = \{ 1, \cdots ,m\}   
	\end{array},
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	where $d_i^R \in {\mathbb{N}}$ is the index of ${R_i}$ and $A_{i,k}^R,k \in \{ 1, \cdots ,p\}$ is the $k$th attribute value of ${R_i}$.  
	
	Likewise, the index and attribute values of ${T_j}$ with $q$ attributes can be denoted as
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:task denote}
	\begin{array}{l}
	(d_j^T,A_{j,1}^T, \cdots ,A_{j,q}^T),{\kern 5pt}j \in \mathcal{J} = \{ 1, \cdots ,n\}  
	\end{array},
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	where $d_j^T \in {\mathbb{N}}$ is the index of ${T_j}$ and $A_{j,k}^T,k \in \{ 1, \cdots ,q\}$ is the $k$th attribute value of ${T_j}$. We put all indexes of resources and tasks into sets collection ${D^R} = \{ d_1^R, \cdots ,d_m^R\}$ and ${D^T} = \{ d_1^T, \cdots ,d_n^T\}$, respectively. 
	
	Take a vehicle routing problem (VRP) with $m$ vehicles and $n$ customers as an example, vehicles are treated as resources and customers as tasks, which are respectively put into sets $R$ and $T$. Accordingly, they can be indexed as ${D^R} = \{ 1,\cdots,m\} $ and ${D^T} = \{ 1,\cdots,n\} $. The capacity, maximum transportation distance, fixed cost, and depart depot can be regarded as the attributes of $R$. The attributes of $T$ may include the demand, service duration, as well as earliest and latest allowed service time. 
	
	%Furthermore, additional data, such as the time matrix $D$, that are not included within the attributes of resources and tasks, can be treated separately.
	
	\subsubsection{Variables}\label{s223}
	
	Derived from the unified solution structure, the assignment or sequence variable can be expressed as
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:decision variable}
	\begin{array}{l}
	X = \{ {X_1},{X_2}, \cdots ,{X_m}\} 
	\end{array},
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	where ${X_i} = \{ {x_{i,1}},{x_{i,2}}, \cdots ,{x_{i,{n_i}}}\} ,i \in \mathcal{I} $ denotes the task subset assigned to resource ${R_i}$. ${n_i}$ signifies the number of available positions for ${R_i}$. ${x_{i,k}},i \in \mathcal{I},k \in {\mathcal{K}_i} = \{ 1, \cdots ,{n_i}\} $ represents the task assigned to the $k$th position of ${R_i}$. Since the index can distinguish different tasks, ${x_{i,k}} \in {D^T}$. When the positions of ${R_i}$ are ordered, ${X_i}$ is an unordered set and can be viewed as an assignment variable; otherwise, ${X_i}$ is an ordered sequence and regarded as a sequence variable. $X$ is consistent with the solution structure and serves as the core decision variable in a COP. Therefore, it is essential to define $X$ for any COP modeled in REMS and the solution structure can be derived from $X$ when solving a COP.
	
	The attribute variables reflect other specific attributes of the solution structure. For example, when the decision variable is a permutation, time-related variables, such as the start and end serve times for tasks at specific resource positions, may need to be optimized. Given that each task has a specific demand, the amount for a task provided by a resource should be determined. For convenience, we first convert the variable $X$ into a binary matrix $Y^C$ and regard it as an attribute variable, where $y_{i,j,k}^C,i \in \mathcal{I},j \in \mathcal{J},k \in {\mathcal{K}_i}$ denotes whether $T_j$ is assigned to the $k$th position of $R_i$ and can be obtained by
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:0-1 decision variable}
	\begin{array}{l}
	y_{i,j,k}^C = \left\{ {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}}
		{1,{\kern 5pt}{\rm{ if }}{\kern 5pt}{x_{i,k}} = d_j^T}\\
		{0,{\kern 5pt}{\rm{ otherwise}}}
		\end{array}} \right.
	\end{array},
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	
	Accordingly, for the above-mentioned VRP, we use ${t_{{j},{j'}}},{j},{j'} \in \{ 0, \cdots ,n \} $ to represent the travel time from ${j}$ to ${j'}$, where $0$ is the index of the depot and  $\{ 1, \cdots ,n\} $ corresponds to the index of tasks. An attribute variable $Y^S$ is employed to represent the start serve times, where $y_{i,j,k}^S, i \in \mathcal{I},j \in \mathcal{J},k \in {\mathcal{K}_i}$ denotes the start serve time for ${T_j}$ in the $k$th position of ${R_i}$ and can be calculated by
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:start serve time}
	\begin{array}{l}
	y_{i,j,k}^S = \left\{ {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}}
		{{t_{0,j}}y_{i,j,k}^C,{\kern 5pt}k = 1}\\
		{\sum\limits_{j' \in \mathcal{J}} {(y_{i,j',k - 1}^S + {t_{j',j}})} y_{i,j,k}^C,{\kern 5pt}k > 1}
		\end{array}} \right.
	\end{array},
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	
	%=====================================================
	%\begin{equation}\label{Eq:start serve time}
	%\begin{array}{l}
	%y_{i,j,k}^S = \left\{ %{\begin{array}{*{20}{c}}
	%	{{t_{0,j}}{\mathbf{1}_{\{ {x_{i,k}} = d_j^T\} }},{\kern 5pt}k = 1}\\
	%	{\sum\limits_{j' \in \mathcal{J}} {(y_{i,j',k - 1}^S + {t_{j',j}})} {\mathbf{1}_{\{ {x_{i,k}} = d_j^T\} }},{\kern 5pt}k > 1}
	%	\end{array}} \right.
	%\end{array},
	%\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	%where $\mathbf{1}{_{\{ A\} }}$ is an indicator function. When condition $A$ is true, then $\mathbf{1}{_{\{ A\} }} = 1$, otherwise, $\mathbf{1}{_{\{ A\} }} = 0$.
	
	As task ${T_j}$ has a serve duration ${s_j}$, the end serve time $y_{i,k}^E$ for $T_j$ located in the $k$th position of $R_i$ can be calculated by
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:end serve time}
	\begin{array}{l}
	y_{i,j,k}^E = (y_{i,j,k}^S + {s_j})y_{i,j,k}^C,{\kern 5pt}i \in \mathcal{I},k \in {\mathcal{K}_i}
	\end{array}.
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	
	When task ${T_j}$ has a demand of ${q_j}$, we use another attribute variable $y_{i,j,k}^Q,i \in I,k \in {K_i}$ to indicate the provided amount of $T_j$ in the $k$th position of ${R_i}$. It can be calculated as
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:serve amount}
	\begin{array}{l}
	y_{i,j,k}^Q = {q_j}y_{i,j,k}^C,{\kern 5pt}i \in \mathcal{I},k \in {\mathcal{K}_i}
	\end{array}.
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	
	%Furthermore, decision variables can be reformulated into alternative forms to simplify and improve the model. For instance, converting a decision variable into an assignment matrix can enable a simpler expression of objective functions and constraints and accelerate the computation process.
	%We represent derived variables as a function about $X$, where the $i$th state variable can be denoted as
	As seen in \eqref{Eq:start serve time}-\eqref{Eq:serve amount}, the attribute variables reflect other aspects of the solution structure and can be expressed as a function of $X$. When we define $r$ attribute variables for a COP, then the $i$th attribute variable can be denoted as
	 %=====================================================
	 \begin{equation}\label{Eq:state variable}
	 \begin{array}{l}
	 {Y_i} = {\psi _i}(X),{\kern 5pt}i \in \{ 1, \cdots ,r\} 
	 \end{array}.
	 \end{equation}

	%=====================================================

	%{Y_i} = {\psi _i}(X)

	\subsubsection{Objectives}\label{s224}
	
	The objective function varies with the problem type and specific requirements. Some frequently occurring objective functions in COPs include minimizing the total cost, maximizing the profit, minimizing the makespan, etc..
	
	For example, given that assigning $T_j$ to the $k$th position of ${R_i}$ will have a cost ${c_{i,j,k}}$, the objective of minimizing the total cost can be
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:total cost of resources}
	\begin{array}{l}
	{\rm{min  }}\sum\limits_{k \in {K_i}} {\sum\limits_{j \in J} {\sum\limits_{i \in I} {{c_{i,j,k}}y_{i,j,k}^C} } } 
	\end{array}
	\end{equation}
	%===================================================== 
	
	Additionally, assume that putting task ${T_j}$ to the $k$th position of resource $R_i$ will generate profit ${p_{i,j,k}}$, then maximizing the profit can be represented as
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:maximize the profit}
	\begin{array}{l}
	{\rm{max  }}\sum\limits_{i \in \mathcal{I}} {\sum\limits_{j \in \mathcal{J}} {\sum\limits_{k \in {\mathcal{K}_i}} {({p_{i,j,k}} - {c_{i,j,k}})y_{i,j,k}^C} } } 
	\end{array}
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	
	%Similarly, when assigning ${T_j}$ to the $k$th position of resource ${R_i}$ will generate cost ${c_{i,j,k}}$, the objective minimizing the total cost can be presented as
	%=====================================================
	%\begin{equation}\label{Eq:minimizing the total cost}
	%\begin{array}{l}
	%{\rm{min  }}\sum\limits_{i \in I} {\sum\limits_{j \in J} {\sum\limits_{k \in {K_i}} {{c_{i,j,k}}{\mathbf{1}_{\{ {x_{i,k}} = d_j^T\} }}} } } 
	%\end{array}
	%\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	
	%For minimizing the makespan, we introduce a attribute variable $Y$, where $Y_{i,k}$ represents the completion time for resource ${R_i}$ on the task located in the $k$th position. As such, the objective can be denoted as
	For minimizing the makespan, we take the above-mentioned VRP as an example. As such, the objective can be denoted as
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:minimize the makespan}
	\begin{array}{l}
	\min \left\{ \max_{i \in \mathcal{I}, j \in \mathcal{J}, k \in \mathcal{K}_i} y_{i,j,k}^E \right\}
	\end{array}
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	
	Overall, as shown in the examples of \eqref{Eq:total cost of resources}-\eqref{Eq:minimize the makespan}, the objective functions can be calculated by variables $X$ and $Y$, i.e.,
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:objective}
	\begin{array}{l}
	{\rm{min {\kern 5pt} or {\kern 5pt} max {\kern 5pt}}}f(X,Y)
	\end{array}
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	
	\subsubsection{Constraints}\label{s225}
	
	The constraints reflect limitations imposed by resources and tasks, encompassing logical relationships, the value ranges of variables, resource capacities, the requirement of tasks on time, space, etc.. Hereafter, some common constraints are expressed.
	
	Firstly, there is a class of constraints that pertain to resources, focusing on their capacities, availability, or limitations. For example, the constraint imposes a limit on the number of tasks assigned to each resource and can be denoted as:
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:resource constraint 1}
	\begin{array}{l}
	\sum\limits_{k \in {\mathcal{K}_i}} {\sum\limits_{j \in \mathcal{J}} {y_{i,j,k}^C} } ( \le , \ge {\rm{or}} = )n_i^R,{\kern 5pt}i \in \mathcal{I}
	\end{array},
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	where $n_i^R$ is the threshold value for the number of tasks assigned to ${R_i}$. The constraint in \eqref{Eq:resource constraint 1} ensures that the number of tasks assigned to ${R_i}$ is no more than, no less than, or equal to $n_i^R$, respectively.
	
	Moreover, if the capacity for resource ${R_i}$ is ${Q_i}$ and the demand for task ${T_j}$ is ${q_j}$, the capacity constraint of resources can be defined as
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:resource constraint 2}
	\begin{array}{l}
	\sum\limits_{k \in {\mathcal{K}_i}} {\sum\limits_{j \in \mathcal{J}} {{q_j}y_{i,j,k}^C} }  \le {Q_i},{\kern 5pt}i \in \mathcal{I}
	\end{array}.
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	
	Furthermore, the constraints presented in \eqref{Eq:resource constraint 1} and \eqref{Eq:resource constraint 2} can be unified as
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:resource constraint 3}
	\begin{array}{l}
	\sum\limits_{k \in {\mathcal{K}_i}} {\sum\limits_{j \in \mathcal{J}} {{\rho _{i,j,k}^R}y_{i,j,k}^C} } ( \le , \ge {\rm{or}} = )\theta_i^R,{\kern 5pt}i \in \mathcal{I}
	\end{array},
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	where $\theta_i^R$ is a threshold value. When ${\rho _{i,j,k}^R} = 1$ and $\theta_i^R = n_i^R$, the constraint can be converted to \eqref{Eq:resource constraint 1} and when ${\rho _{i,j,k}^R} = {q_j},i \in \mathcal{I},k \in {\mathcal{K}_i}$ and $\theta_i^R = {Q_i}$, it becomes constraint \eqref{Eq:resource constraint 2}.
	
	Additionally, some constraints focus on task limitations. For instance, the constraint specifying that task ${T_j}$ must be executed no more than, no less than, or exactly $n_j^T$ times on all resources $R$ can be denoted as
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:task constraint 1}
	\begin{array}{l}
	\sum\limits_{i \in \mathcal{I}} {\sum\limits_{k \in {\mathcal{K}_i}} {y_{i,j,k}^C} } ( \le , \ge {\rm{or}} = )n_j^T,{\kern 5pt}j \in \mathcal{J}
	\end{array},
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	
	The constraints like \eqref{Eq:task constraint 1} can further unified as:
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:task constraint 2}
	\begin{array}{l}
	\sum\limits_{k \in {\mathcal{K}_i}} {\sum\limits_{i \in \mathcal{I}} {{\rho _{i,j,k}^T}y_{i,j,k}^C} } ( \le , \ge {\rm{or}} = )\theta_i^T,{\kern 5pt}j \in \mathcal{J}
	\end{array},
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	where $\theta_i^T$ indicates the threshold value. When $\theta_i^T = n_j^T$ and ${\rho _{i,j,k}^T} = 1$, it can be constraint \eqref{Eq:task constraint 1}. 
	
	When it comes to the logical relationship between tasks, it may be necessary to specify whether tasks ${T_{{j}}}$ and ${T_{{j'}}}$ must be executed on the same resource or on different resources. This can be expressed as
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:logical constraint 1}
	\begin{array}{l}
	\sum\limits_{k \in {{\cal K}_i}} {y_{i,j',k}^C}  = 0 {\kern 5pt}{\rm{ or }}{\kern 5pt} 1,{\kern 5pt}{\rm{ if }}\sum\limits_{k \in {{\cal K}_i}} {y_{i,j,k}^C}  = 1,j \ne j' \in {\cal J},i \in {\cal I}
	\end{array},
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	
	Some COPs impose constraints on the order of task execution. If task ${T_{{j'}}}$ must be arranged before ${T_{{j}}}$, then it can be denoted as:
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:logical constraint 2}
	\begin{array}{r}
	\sum\limits_{k' \in \{ 1, \cdots ,k - 1\} } {y_{i,j,k}^C}  = 1,{\rm{ {\kern 5pt} if {\kern 5pt} }}{x_{i,k}} = d_{{j'}}^T,i \in \mathcal{I},\\
	{j} \ne {j'} \in \mathcal{J},k \in {\mathcal{K}_i}
	\end{array},
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	
	A class of constraints further articulates the relationships between resources and tasks. For example, the constraint that task ${T_j}$ needs to be no more than, no less than, or executed exactly $n_{i,j}^T$ on resource ${R_i}$ can be
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:resource-task constraint 1}
	\begin{array}{l}
	\sum\limits_{k \in {K_i}} {y_{i,j,k}^C} ( \le , \ge {\rm{or}} = )n_{i,j}^T,{\kern 5pt}i \in \mathcal{I},j \in \mathcal{J}
	\end{array},
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	
	The constraints such as \eqref{Eq:resource-task constraint 1} can be further unified as
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:resource-task constraint 2}
	\begin{array}{l}
	\sum\limits_{k \in {K_i}} {{\rho_{i,j,k}}y_{i,j,k}^C} ( \le , \ge {\rm{or}} = )\theta_{i,j},{\kern 5pt}i \in \mathcal{I},j \in \mathcal{J}
	\end{array},
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	where $\theta_{i,j}$ is the threshold value and ${\rho_{i,j,k}}$ denotes the coefficient matrix. If the $\theta_{i,j}{\rm{ = }}n_{i,j}^T$ and ${\rho_{i,j,k}}{\rm{ = }}1$, \eqref{Eq:resource-task constraint 2} can be converted into \eqref{Eq:resource-task constraint 1}.
	
	Similar to the objective function, constraints can also be expressed in terms of variables $X$ and $Y$, as in \eqref{Eq:resource constraint 1}-\eqref{Eq:resource-task constraint 2}. When these constraints are categorized into equality and inequality constraints, they can be denoted as \eqref{Eq:equality and inequality constraints}.
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:equality and inequality constraints}
	\begin{array}{l}
	\left\{ {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}}
		{{g_i}(X,Y) \le 0,{\kern 5pt}i \in \{ 1, \cdots ,l\} }\\
		{{h_i}(X,Y) = 0,{\kern 5pt}i \in \{ l + 1, \cdots ,z\} }
		\end{array}} \right.
	\end{array},
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	where ${g}(X,Y)$ and ${h}(X,Y)$ denote the inequality and equality constraints, respectively.
	
	To evaluate the constraint for a solution, the $i$th constraint value can be calculated as
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:constraints}
	\begin{array}{l}
	{G_i}(X,Y) = \left\{ {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}}
		{\max \{ 0,{g_i}(X,Y)\} ,{\kern 5pt}i \in \{ 1, \ldots ,l\} }\\
		{|{h_i}(X,Y)|,{\kern 5pt}i \in \{ l + 1 \ldots ,z\} }
		\end{array}} \right.
	\end{array},
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	
	
	Overall, under the requirement that resources and tasks remain discrete and unchanged, we propose a unified solution structure for a general COP. The assignment or sequence variable is expressed in a standardized form, as seen in \eqref{Eq:decision variable}. Nevertheless, the attribute variables can be freely defined with no type and structure requirement, as long as they can be obtained from $X$. Furthermore, we impose no specific requirements on the form of the objective and constraint functions as well. Instead, we only require that these functions provide a quantifiable value for evaluating a solution.
	
	\section{Design of metaheuristic algorithms}\label{s3}
	
	Solving a COP requires determining the best assignment for the variable defined in \eqref{Eq:decision variable} and \eqref{Eq:state variable} to achieve the objective in \eqref{Eq:objective} adhering to the constraints outlined in \eqref{Eq:constraints}. Metaheuristic algorithms typically begin with one or more initial solutions, then iteratively generate new solutions and explore solution space by neighborhood perturbation, crossover, destroy and repair, or other operators. In each iteration, the best-so-far solution and current solutions are accordingly updated based on ranking and selection strategies. The section will design various fundamental operators in terms of the features of metaheuristics and the characteristics of the COPs modeled in Section~\ref{s2}, thereby facilitating the design of metaheuristic algorithms including the single-point-based and population-based algorithms. 
	
	\subsection{Solution Structure}\label{s31}
	
	As illustrated in Fig.~\ref{Fig:modeling framework}, we only need to search the solution structure during the process of optimization, which is automatically defined according to the assignment or sequence variable $X$. The solution structure is further illustrated in Fig.~\ref{Fig:solution structure}. We refer to assigning a task to a specific position within a resource as a unit assignment. All unit assignments for a resource form a sub-assignment. The sub-assignments for all resources constitute a solution. Corresponding to the assignment or sequence variable, as $X_i$ is a sequence variable and the positions of ${R_i}$ are ordered, the sub-assignment of ${R_i}$ is an ordered sequence. When $X_i$ is a assignment variable, the sub-assignment is an unordered set.

	\subsection{Initial Solution}\label{s32}
	
	An initial solution is generated by a constructive heuristic method, where unit assignments are determined incrementally starting from an empty solution. To ensure feasibility, each unit assignment should be inserted into the solution without violating constraints until no further feasible unit assignments can be inserted. Determining the feasible unit assignment, i.e., feasible resources, tasks, and positions, in each step is the core of constructing an initial solution. To avoid searching the infeasible unit assignments, we preliminarily determine the feasible unit assignment using some common constraints information presented in Section~\ref{s225}. Determining a feasible unit assignment for a current solution is displayed in Fig.~\ref{Fig:feasible assigment}.
	
	%Determining the feasible unit assignment, i.e., feasible resources, tasks, and positions, in each step is the core of constructing an initial solution. To avoid searching the infeasible unit assignments, we preliminarily determine the feasible unit assignment using some common constraints information in Section~\ref{s224}. Determining a feasible unit assignment for a current solution is displayed in Fig.~\ref{Fig:feasible assigment}.
	
	  %displays how to insert a feasible unit assignment into a current solution. We preliminarily determine the feasible unit assignment to avoid searching for the infeasible space .
	%=====================================================
	\begin{figure}[htb]
		\begin{center}		\subfigure{\psfig{file=figures/feasible_assignment.eps, width=3.6in}}
		\end{center}
		\caption{Determine a feasible unit assignment for a current solution.}\label{Fig:feasible assigment}
	\end{figure}
	%======================================================
	
	Firstly, a feasible resource set ${FR}$ is identified from the current solution according to the constraints in \eqref{Eq:resource constraint 3}. Following this, a resource ${R_i}$ is randomly selected from ${FR}$. Subsequently, in terms of the constraints in \eqref{Eq:task constraint 2}, \eqref{Eq:logical constraint 1}, and \eqref{Eq:resource-task constraint 2}, we determine the feasible task set $FT_i$ for ${R_i}$. A task ${T_j}$ is then randomly selected from $FT_i$. When ${S_i}$ is an unordered set, the insertable position is ${A} = \{ |{S_i}| + 1\} $. Conversely, if ${S_i}$ is an ordered sequence, the insertable position is ${A} = \{ 1, \cdots ,|{S_i}| + 1\} $. Based on constraints in \eqref{Eq:logical constraint 2}, the feasible positions $FP_{i,j} \subseteq {A}$ are further determined. Subsequently, the best position ${p_k}$, that enables the best solution among $FP_{i,j}$, is selected. If the unit assignment of assigning ${T_j}$ to position ${p_k}$ of ${R_i}$ enables an equal or better solution, then the current solution is updated by inserting the unit assignment.
	%Inserting a task into the $k$th position will cause the original tasks in the $k$th position and all subsequent tasks to shift one position backward. 
	
	Algorithm~\ref{PC:feasible assignment} outlines the process for determining a unit assignment for the current solution $S$. Before generating an initial solution, infeasible resource set $inR$ and infeasible task sets $inT_i,i \in \mathcal{I}$ are initially empty. Lines 1-2 select a resource ${R_i}$ from ${FR}$ and lines 3-4 randomly select a task ${T_j}$ from $FT_i$. Lines 5 assign ${T_j}$ to the best position of ${R_i}$, thereby forming ${S_{\rm{candi}}}$. In lines 6-13, if ${S_{\rm{candi}}}$ is no worse than $S$, then the new unit assignment is accepted. Otherwise, the new unit assignment will be rejected. Accordingly, $inR$ and $inT_i,i \in \mathcal{I}$ should be updated.
	%=============================================================
	\begin{algorithm}[htp]
		\caption{\textbf{Function} \emph{FeasibleAssignment}()}\label{PC:feasible assignment}
		\KwIn{Problem model, current solution $S$, $in{R}$, and $inT_i,i \in \mathcal{I}$.}
		\KwOut{${S_{\rm{new}}}$, $inR$, and $inT_i,i \in \mathcal{I}$.}
		\LinesNumbered
		Identify ${FR}$ for ${S}$ and ${FR} \leftarrow {FR}\backslash in{R}$ \;
		Randomly select a resource ${R_i}$ from ${FR}$\;
		Determine $FT_i$ and $FT_i \leftarrow FT_i\backslash inT_i$\;
		Randomly select a task ${T_j}$ from $FT_i$\;
		Insert the ${T_j}$ into the best position of ${R_i}$ for ${S}$ and form ${S_{\rm{candi}}}$\;
		\If{${S_{\rm{candi}}}$ is no worse than ${S}$}{
			${S_{\rm{new}}} \leftarrow {S_{\rm{candi}}}$\;
			\If{${S_i}$ is an ordered sequence}{
				$inT_i \leftarrow \emptyset $\;
			}
			}
		\Else{
			${S_{\rm{new}}} \leftarrow S$, and $inT_i \leftarrow inT_i \cup {T_j}$ \;
			\If{$T\backslash inT_i = \emptyset $}{
				$in{R} \leftarrow in{R} \cup {R_i}$\;
			}
		}		
	\end{algorithm}
	%============================================================= 
	
	In terms of Algorithm~\ref{PC:feasible assignment}, Algorithm~\ref{PC:Initial Solution} displays the procedure for generating an initial solution. Line 1 initializes the solution as an empty set. Subsequently, in lines 2-4, tasks are iteratively assigned to available positions on resources until no feasible unit assignments can be inserted.
	%=============================================================
	\begin{algorithm}[htp]
		\caption{\textbf{Function} \emph{InitialSolution}()}\label{PC:Initial Solution}
		\KwIn{Problem model.}
		\KwOut{Initial solution $S$.}
		\LinesNumbered
		Initialize ${S_i} \leftarrow \emptyset ,i \in \mathcal{I}$, $in{R} \leftarrow \emptyset $, and $inT_i \leftarrow \emptyset ,i \in \mathcal{I}$\;
		\While{$R\backslash inR \ne \emptyset $}{
			$[S,inR,inT_i,i \in \mathcal{I}] \leftarrow $\emph{FeasibleAssignment}()\;
		}
	\end{algorithm}
	%=============================================================
	
	\subsection{Neighborhood Structure}\label{s33}
	
	The neighborhood structure is utilized to perturb the current solution, which is widely used for neighborhood-based algorithms such as VNS, SA, and TS. To efficiently solve diverse COPs, the designed neighborhood structures must accommodate the specific characteristics of different COPs. We propose the following six types of neighborhood structures based on the unified solution structure.
	
	\begin{itemize}
		\item \emph{Swap}: It selects two sets of tasks, each containing 1-2 consecutive tasks from either the same resource or two different resources, and swaps them.
		
		\item \emph{Shift}: It first selects a set of tasks from a resource and then shifts it to other positions within the same resource or to different resources. To promote a diverse neighborhood structure, when shifting within the same resource, the selected task set contains 1-2 consecutive tasks. When shifting across different resources, the selected task set may consist of either 1-2 consecutive tasks or all tasks from the resource. 
		
		\item \emph{Remove}: This operation selects a task and removes it from the current solution.
		
		\item \emph{Insert}: It selects a task that is not currently presented in the solution and inserts it into another feasible position.
		
		\item \emph{Remove and insert}: It involves selecting a set with 1-2 consecutive tasks to remove. Subsequently, other feasible tasks that do not exist in the current solution are inserted.
		
		\item \emph{Reverse}: It selects a set of tasks within a resource or across two resources, and reverses the order of these tasks. The reversed tasks are then inserted according to their new order.
		
	\end{itemize}
	
	Among these neighborhood structures, the insert operation should be performed without increasing any constraint value to ensure the feasibility of a neighborhood solution.
	
	It should be noted that some neighborhood structures may be useless or inefficient for a specific COP. For example, when $X$ is an assignment variable, the neighborhood structures that perform within the same resource are useless. Therefore, to enable better utilization of neighborhood structures, an adaptive selection strategy for neighborhood structures is employed. 
	
	In the selection strategy, the selection probability for the $i$th neighborhood structure can be denoted as $p_i,i \in \{ 1, \cdots, {ns} \} $, where $ns$ is the number of neighborhood structures. $p_i$ changes with the success times $sc_i$ and selected times $st_i$ during a specific consecutive iteration. At the beginning of optimization, $p_i = 1,sc_i, st_i = 0,i \in \{ 1, \cdots, {ns} \} $. During the optimization, $p_i$ will be updated by
	%=====================================================
	\begin{equation}\label{Eq:neighborhood selection}
	\begin{array}{l}
	{p_i} = s{c_i}/s{t_i},i \in \{ 1, \cdots, {ns} \} .
	\end{array}
	\end{equation}
	%=====================================================
	
	Algorithm~\ref{PC:Neighborhood Solution} displays the pseudocode for generating a neighborhood solution ${S_{\rm{neighbor}}}$ of the current solution $S$. We first select a neighborhood structure to generate a neighborhood solution according to the roulette selection for $p_i,i \in \{ 1, \cdots, {ns} \} $. As presented in lines 1-2, when $p_i = 0,\forall i \in \{ 1, \cdots, {ns}\} $, they should be reinitialized to 1. In lines 5-7, $sc_i$ and $st_i$ should be updated after using a neighborhood structure. When the total selected times for all neighborhood structures are equal to a set iteration ${\rm{MaxIter}}1$ in line 10, $p_i$ will be updated by \eqref{Eq:neighborhood selection}.
	%=============================================================
	\begin{algorithm}[htp]
		\caption{\textbf{Function} \emph{NeighborhoodSolution}()}\label{PC:Neighborhood Solution}
		\KwIn{Problem model, $S$, $p_i$, $sc_i$, $st_i$, $\forall i \in \{ 1, \cdots, {ns} \} $.}
		\KwOut{${S_{\rm{neighbor}}}$,  $p_i,sc_i, st_i, \forall i \in \{ 1, \cdots, ns\} $.}
		\LinesNumbered
		\If{$p_i = 0,\forall i \in \{ 1, \cdots ,{ns}\} $}{
			$p_i \leftarrow 1,i \in \{ 1, \cdots ,{ns}\} $ \;
		}
		Select a neighborhood structure $i$ by the roulette selection of $p_i,i \in \{ 1, \cdots, {ns} \} $\;
		Generate a neighborhood solution $S_{\rm{neighbor}}$ of $S$ by the $i$th neighborhood structure\;
		$st_i \leftarrow st_i + 1$\;
		\If{${S_{\rm{neighbor}}}$ is better than $S$}{
			$sc_i \leftarrow sc_i + 1$ \;
		}
		\While{$\sum\limits_{i \in \{ 1, \cdots ,{ns}\} } {s{t_i}}  = {\rm{MaxIter}}1$}{
			Update $P$ by \eqref{Eq:neighborhood selection}\;
			$st_i,sc_i \leftarrow 0,i \in \{ 1, \cdots ,{ns}\} $ \;
		}
	\end{algorithm}
	%=============================================================
	
	\subsection{Destroy-and-Repair Operators}\label{s34}
	
	The destroy operator randomly selects a subset of $nd$ tasks from the current solution $S$ and removes them, forming a destroy solution ${S_{\rm{destroy}}}$. Subsequently, the repair operator is applied to iteratively reinsert feasible tasks into the best positions of ${S_{\rm{destroy}}}$, forming a repair solution ${S_{\rm{repair}}}$. The destroy-and-repair procedure is outlined in Algorithm~\ref{PC:Destroy Repair}, where the process of generating a repair solution is similar to that in Algorithm~\ref{PC:Initial Solution}, with the current solution being treated as ${S_{\rm{destroy}}}$.
	%=============================================================
	\begin{algorithm}[htp]
		\caption{\textbf{Function} \emph{DestroyRepair}()}\label{PC:Destroy Repair}
		\KwIn{Problem model, $S$.}
		\KwOut{${S_{\rm{destroy}}}$.}
		\LinesNumbered
		Randomly remove ${nd}$ tasks from $S$, the resulting solution is recorded as ${S_{\rm{destroy}}}$\;
		${S_{\rm{repair}}} \leftarrow {S_{\rm{destroy}}}$, $inR \leftarrow \emptyset $, and $inT_i \leftarrow \emptyset ,i \in \mathcal{I}$ \;
		\While{$R\backslash inR \ne \emptyset $}{
			$[{S_{\rm{repair}}},inR,inT_i,i \in \mathcal{I}] \leftarrow $ \emph{FeasibleAssignment}()\;
		}
	\end{algorithm}
	%=============================================================
	
	\subsection{Crossover Operator}\label{s35}
	
	We design a single-point crossover for COPs with a single resource and a two-point crossover for those with multiple resources. As presented in Fig.~\ref{Fig:Single-point crossover}, the single-point crossover randomly selects a crossover point for Parents 1 and 2. The offspring inherits the unit assignments from Parent 1 before the crossover point. The tasks from Parent 2 after the crossover point are added sequentially, ensuring that no constraints are violated. If the offspring can be further improved by task insertion, the repair operation outlined in Algorithm~\ref{PC:Destroy Repair} is applied to refine the solution.
	%=====================================================
	\begin{figure}[htb]
		\begin{center}	\subfigure{\psfig{file=figures/Single-point_crossover.eps, width=3.6in}}
		\end{center}
		\caption{Single-point crossover for COPs with a single resource.}\label{Fig:Single-point crossover}
	\end{figure}
	%======================================================
	
	Fig.~\ref{Fig:Two-point crossover} illustrates the process of generating offspring by a two-point crossover. Two crossover points are randomly selected from Parents 1 and 2. The offspring inherits the sub-assignments outside the two crossover points from Parent 1. The sub-assignments between the two points are inherited from Parent 2, where each unit assignment is added to the offspring without violating any constraints. Similar to the single-point crossover, the repair operation is employed to further insert feasible unit assignments to ensure the feasibility of offspring.
	%=====================================================
	\begin{figure}[htb]
		\begin{center}		\subfigure{\psfig{file=figures/Two-point_crossover.eps, width=3.6in}}
		\end{center}
		\caption{Two-point crossover for COPs with multiple resources.}\label{Fig:Two-point crossover}
	\end{figure}
	%======================================================
	
	Algorithm~\ref{PC:Crossover Operation} presents the procedure of the crossover operation for a population $pop$. Each individual in $pop$ is sequentially selected as Parent 1, while Parent 2 is chosen from $pop\backslash {\rm{Parent }}1$ using a 2-tournament selection strategy. After generating the offspring for all individuals in $pop$ based on crossover rate $\alpha $, $offspring$ will be output.
	%=============================================================
	\begin{algorithm}[htp]
		\caption{\textbf{Function} \emph{CrossoverOperation}()}\label{PC:Crossover Operation}
		\KwIn{Problem model, $pop$.}
		\KwOut{$offspring$.}
		\LinesNumbered
		\For{$po{p_i} = pop$}{
			${\rm{Parent }}1 \leftarrow po{p_i}$, and $offsprin{g_i} \leftarrow {\rm{Parent }}1$\;
			\If{${\rm{rand}} < {\alpha}$}{
				${\rm{Parent 2}}$ is selected from $pop\backslash {\rm{Parent }}1$ by the 2-tournament selection\;
				\If{$n = 1$}{
					Generate $offsprin{g_i}$ by the single-point crossover;
				}
				\Else{
					Generate $offsprin{g_i}$ by the two-point crossover;
				}
			}
		}
	\end{algorithm}
	%=============================================================
	
	\subsection{Assess and Ranking}\label{s36}
	
	Despite efforts to obtain feasible solutions during the iterative process, the diverse attributes of a COP and the limitations of operators may still lead to infeasible solutions. Considering this, taking a COP with a minimum objective as an example, we propose the following rules to compare two solutions ${S}$ and ${S'}$, where ${X}$, $Y$ and ${X'}$, $Y'$ are the variables of ${S}$ and ${S'}$, respectively. 
	
	\begin{itemize}
		\item  If ${S}$ is a feasible solution and ${S'}$ is an infeasible solution, then ${S}$ is considered better than ${S'}$.
		
		\item As both ${S}$ and ${S'}$ are feasible solutions, we compare them in terms of the objective function values. If $f({X, Y}) < f({X', Y'})$, then ${S}$ is better than ${S'}$.
		
		\item When both ${S}$ and ${S'}$ are infeasible solutions, their quality is assessed by first comparing the constraints and then the objective function values. To evaluate the constraints, a fast non-dominated sorting strategy is employed. If
		%=====================================================
		\begin{equation}\label{Eq:sorting strategy}
		\begin{array}{l}
		{G_i}({X}, Y) < {G_i}({X'}, Y'),{\kern 5pt}\exists i \in \{ 1, \cdots ,z\} {\kern 5pt}{\rm{and}} \\
		{G_i}({X}, Y) \le {G_i}({X'}, Y'),{\kern 5pt}\forall i \in \{ 1, \cdots ,z\},
		\end{array}
		\end{equation}
		%=====================================================
		we consider ${S}$ dominating ${S'}$, indicating ${S}$ to be better than ${S'}$. Otherwise, we consider them to have a non-dominated relationship, meaning they are equivalent in terms of constraints. In this case, the quality of the two solutions cannot be determined by constraints alone, prompting a further comparison of their objective function values. For objective functions, if $f({X, Y}) < f({X', Y'})$, then ${S}$ is better than ${S'}$.
	\end{itemize}
	
	Based on the above comparison rules, we propose a hierarchical ranking method to rank multiple solutions. As illustrated in Fig.~\ref{Fig:ranking method}, firstly, feasible solutions always receive better ranking values than infeasible solutions. Within the feasible solutions, the ranking values are further refined based on their objective function values, with better objective function values receiving better rankings. The infeasible solutions will be layered in terms of the number of other solutions they dominate, where a solution with a better ranking value can dominate a greater number of other solutions. Within the same constraint level, the solutions are further ranked based on their objective function values.
	%=====================================================
	\begin{figure}[htb]
		\begin{center}\subfigure{\psfig{file=figures/ranking_method.eps, width=3.6in}}
		\end{center}
		\caption{A hierarchical ranking method for multiple solutions.}\label{Fig:ranking method}
	\end{figure}

	\subsection{Framework of Metaheuristic Algorithms}\label{s37}
	
	Based on the aforementioned operators, various metaheuristic algorithms can be constructed. Herein, we develop two metaheuristics frameworks, i.e., a single-point-based framework and a population-based (genetic algorithm) framework.
	
	The pseudocode for the single-point search metaheuristic framework is provided in Algorithm~\ref{PC:Single-point-based Metaheuristic}. 
	%=============================================================
	\begin{algorithm}[htp]
		\caption{\textbf{Main Procedure of Single-point-based Metaheuristic Framework}}\label{PC:Single-point-based Metaheuristic}
		\KwIn{Problem model.}
		\KwOut{Best-so-far solution ${S_{{\rm{best}}}}$.}
		\LinesNumbered
		${S_{\rm{initial}}} \leftarrow $\emph{InitialSolution}()\;
		Initialize $NIter \leftarrow 0$, $Iter \leftarrow 0$, and other parameters\;
		Initialize current solution $S \leftarrow {S_{\rm{initial}}}$ and ${S_{{\rm{best}}}} \leftarrow {S_{\rm{initial}}}$\;
		\While{termination condition is not satisfied}{
			New solution set $C \leftarrow \emptyset $\;
			\While{$|C| < N$}{
				Generate a new solution ${S_{{\rm{new}}}}$\;
				\If{${S_{{\rm{new}}}} \ne \emptyset $}{
					$C \leftarrow C \cup {S_{{\rm{new}}}}$\;
				}
			}
			Select the best solution ${S_{\rm{subopt}}}$ from $C$\;
			\If{${S_{\rm{subopt}}}$ is better than ${S_{{\rm{best}}}}$}{
				${S_{{\rm{best}}}} \leftarrow {S_{\rm{subopt}}}$ and $NIter \leftarrow 0$\;
			}
			\Else{
				$NIter \leftarrow NIter + 1$
			}
			$Iter \leftarrow Iter + J$\;
			Accept ${S_{{\rm{subopt}}}}$ as the current solution $S$ in terms of an acceptance criterion\;
			\If{$NIter = {\rm{MaxIter2}}$}{
				Regenerate the current solution\;
			}
		}
	\end{algorithm}
	%=============================================================
	
	Algorithm~\ref{PC:Single-point-based Metaheuristic} begins with the generation of an initial solution ${S_{\rm{initial}}}$ in line 1. Both the parameter $NIter$, which tracks the number of consecutive iterations without improvement, and the total iteration number $Iter$ are initialized to 0. Additionally, specific metaheuristic methods may require the initialization of specific parameters. Subsequently, both current solution $S$ and best-so-far solution ${S_{{\rm{best}}}}$ are initialized to ${S_{{\rm{initial}}}}$. In each loop, a new solution set $C$ containing $N$ solutions is generated, as detailed in lines 5-9. If the best solution ${S_{{\rm{subopt}}}}$ in $C$ outperforms ${S_{{\rm{best}}}}$, the latter is updated to ${S_{{\rm{subopt}}}}$, and $NIter$ is updated accordingly in lines 11-14. Furthermore, $S$ is updated based on an acceptance criterion. The algorithm terminates and outputs ${S_{{\rm{best}}}}$ once the stopping condition is satisfied. To instantiate the single-point metaheuristic framework, we adopt VNS, TS, LNS, and SA. A detailed introduction about how to realize them in terms of Algorithm~\ref{PC:Single-point-based Metaheuristic} is displayed in Supplementary Material.
	
	% To instantiate the single-point metaheuristic framework, we adopt VNS, TS, LNS, and SA. Among them, VNS, TS, and SA utilize Algorithm~\ref{PC:Neighborhood Solution} to generate a new solution. Specifically, VNS generates a single new solution per iteration, whereas TS and SA are set to produce multiple new solutions herein. In contrast, LNS employs Algorithm~\ref{PC:Destroy Repair} to destroy and repair the current solution and generate a new solution. When Algorithm~\ref{PC:Destroy Repair} cannot improve a current solution within $NIter$ iterations, Algorithm~\ref{PC:Neighborhood Solution} will be applied in the following multiple iterations for LNS.

	Algorithm~\ref{PC:Genetic Algorithm} outlines the main procedure of GA. In lines 1-2, the population $pop$ is generated by Algorithm~\ref{PC:Initial Solution}. Lines 6-9 focus on generating offspring for $pop$ by crossover and mutation by Algorithm~\ref{PC:Crossover Operation} and~\ref{PC:Neighborhood Solution}, respectively. 	\section{Experimental Study}\label{s4}
	
	\subsection{Test Suit and Parameter Setting}\label{s41}
	
	To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposal, 10 COPs are selected including multi-depot vehicle routing problem with time windows (MDVRPTW) \cite{zhen2009hybrid}, vehicle routing problem with pickup and delivery (VRPPD) \cite{van2001comparing}, generalized assignment problem (GAP) \cite{osman1995heuristics}, capacitated facility location problem (CFLP) \cite{sridharan1995capacitated}, bin packing problem with conflicts (BPPC) \cite{muritiba2010algorithms}, generalized bin packing problem (GBPPI) \cite{baldi2019generalized}, quadratic multiple knapsack problem (QMKP) \cite{galli2021polynomial}, high school timetabling problem (HTS) \cite{saviniec2017effective}, job shop scheduling problem (JSSP) \cite{taillard1993benchmarks}, and graph coloring problem (GC) \cite{fleurent1996genetic}. This selection encompasses classical problems like JSSP and GC, generalized problems such as GAP, CFLP, and GBPPI, and variants of classical problems like MDVRPTW, VRPPD, BPPC, QMKP, and HTS. 
	
	The introduction and resource-centered modeling for each type of COPs are provided in Supplementary Material. There is no need for a specialized algorithm design for a COP and the embedded metaheuristic algorithms in REMS are adopted to solve the model.
	
	We execute the experiment for 5 metaheuristic algorithms, GUROBI, SCIP, as well as Routing Solver and CP-SAT of OR-TOOLS on 10 test suits, where COPs are respectively modeled into the suitable form. We do not specifically improve the algorithm herein. Instead, the experiments primarily evaluate the effectiveness and generality of the modeling and algorithm design. Furthermore, since the impact of parameters on algorithm performance is not a primary focus of the paper, we fix the algorithm parameters to specific values. Detailed parameter settings are provided in the Supplementary Material. 
	
	To guarantee a fair comparison, each instance on all algorithms possesses the same maximum running time, which is stated in Supplementary Material as well. Moreover, we repeatedly run 5 times for each algorithm on each problem for the sake of reliability. 
	
	The detailed experimental results are presented in Table S-11 to S-20 of Supplementary Material, including the best and mean objective function values and the best and mean gap values over 5 runs. Among them, the lower bound for each problem is obtained by GUROBI within 3,600 seconds using the default settings.
	
	\subsection{Compare Metaheuristic Algorithms in REMS on Different Problems}\label{s42}
	
	The subsection compares the embedded 5 metaheuristic algorithms in REMS introduced in Section~\ref{s3} across 10 problem types, evaluating their effectiveness in solving various COPs and identifying which algorithm performs best for each instance and problem type.
	
	To evaluate the performance of algorithms on specific instances for each problem type, Fig. S-1 illustrates the radar chart of the mean gap values obtained by 5 metaheuristic algorithms in REMS across 10 problems. Among these charts, a point closer to the center of the circle indicates better mean gap values achieved by an algorithm for a given instance.
	
	The experimental results presented in Table S-11 to S-20 and Fig. S-1 reveal the performance of a metaheuristic algorithm in REMS varies not only within the same problem type but also across different problem types. The observation is consistent with the No Free Lunch (NFL) theorem, which states that no single algorithm can perform optimally across all problems.
	
	Within a single problem type, the results differ across individual instances. For example, LNS outperforms the other algorithms on most MDVRPTW instances. However, for the instances such as MDVRPTW01, 02, 05-08, and 11, LNS may provide worse results compared to some other algorithms. Similarly, although GA generally performs worse on most MDVRPTW instances, GA outperforms certain algorithms on the instances including MDVRPTW01, 07, 11-14, and 16-19. Additionally, the experimental results differ across different problem types. Particularly, LNS performs better across the majority of problem types. However, it performs poorly in most GBPPI instances.

	\subsection{Compare Metaheuristic Algorithms with Other Solvers}\label{s43}
	
	This subsection compares 5 metaheuristic algorithms in REMS with other solvers, including CP-SAT and Routing solvers from OR-TOOLS, SCIP, and GUROBI. Among them, GUROBI and SCIP are exact algorithm-based solvers, while CP-SAT and Routing solvers are mainly heuristic-based. Moreover, GUROBI is a commercial solver, while SCIP is open-source. The Routing solver, specifically designed for vehicle routing problems, is exclusively applied to MDVRPTW and VRPPD. In contrast, CP-SAT is not suitable for problems with non-integer variables, and therefore, it is excluded from solving MDVRPTW and VRPPD herein.
	
	The radar chart of the mean gap values obtained by 8 algorithms on 10 problems is presented in Fig.~\ref{Fig:Radar chart for 8 algorithms}. 
	
	
	According to Table S-11 to S-20 and Fig.~\ref{Fig:Radar chart for 8 algorithms}, the results reveal that compared to the exact algorithm-based solvers, i.e., GUROBI and SCIP, 5 metaheuristic algorithms in REMS can obtain better solutions, especially for large-scale instances and complex problems. Notably, 5 metaheuristic algorithms in REMS outperform GUROBI and SCIP in all instances of MDVRPTW and VRPPD. Additionally, when it comes to BPPC, GBPPI, and GC, although GUROBI can provide better or equal results, it fails to find any feasible solutions for some large-scale instances. Meanwhile, SCIP is able to obtain feasible solutions for most BPPC and GC, but these solutions are not superior to those found by the metaheuristic algorithms. Regarding QMKP, the emergence of the quadratic objective function makes the metaheuristic algorithms in REMS outperform GUROBI and SCIP in most QMKP instances. Concerning HTS, which involves complex objectives and constraints, the 5 metaheuristic algorithms of REMS consistently yield better solutions than GUROBI and SCIP for the majority of instances. Furthermore, the solutions provided by GUROBI and SCIP are relatively stable over different runs, but they remain a certain randomness due to the employment of some heuristic rules in GUROBI and SCIP.
	
	In comparison with OR-TOOLS, the experimental results obtained by the algorithms in REMS are worse in most instances. On the one hand, OR-TOOLS exhibits good performance on some relatively large-scale instances including GC21-30, BPPC11-20, and 51-60. This can be attributed to the effective incorporation of various heuristic methods. On the other hand, it also performs well in problems that benefit from its specific modeling approach and algorithmic design, such as VRPPD and JSSP. However, the 5 algorithms in REMS are mainly based on classical metaheuristic algorithms. Therefore, due to the limitation of classical metaheuristic methods in REMS and the integration of advanced techniques and problem-specific knowledge in modeling and algorithm design, the performance of the algorithms in REMS is not as good as OR-TOOLS in most instances.
	
	Nevertheless, an interesting observation is that the embedded metaheuristic algorithms in REMS have the potential to locate better solutions for several problems with complex objectives and constraints, including MDVRPTW, HTS, and QMKP. Regarding MDVRPTW, OR-TOOLS fails to locate any feasible solutions in the instances excluding MDVRPTW07, 09, 16, 17, and 19, whereas 5 metaheuristic algorithms in REMS can realize it. Additionally, due to the complexity of HTS, the solutions produced by OR-TOOLS are inferior to those obtained by REMS for most instances.
